title: [Chapitre] III. Réseaux via découpages : notes manuscrites (08/06/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
This is the last page of the chapter 'Réseaux via découpages' (1986). The setting from p.39 is a 'tame' (modéré) one-dimensional object L: a line or interval. Finite families of mutually tame parts of L have boundary points forming a totally ordered finite set t1<...<tn. The Boolean algebra they generate depends only on this 'découpage' (subdivision) of L. Its atoms are the convex pieces [L<t1], {t1}, ]t1,t2[, ..., {tn}, [L>tn].

On p.40 Grothendieck asks how to characterize an ordered interval as a 'réseau' (a network or 1-dimensional combinatorial object) using only unordered data:
- A set S ⊂ P_2(L) of 2-element subsets. He writes it as equal to something like Drap_2(L) (?), i.e. the 'admissible' pairs or 2-flags.
- For each ε={a,b} in S, the subset L^ε = {x in L | {a,x}, {b,x} in S}.
- A decomposition of L^ε into 'connected components' via an equivalence relation R_ε.

The intended content is that the ordered structure (up to reversal) can be recovered from incidence and separation data. Roughly, x lies between a and b exactly when a and b fall into different components after x is removed, or when x lies in a distinguished component of L^ε. He starts the exercise but stops. He judges that it must be classical ('Hilbert?') in the totally ordered case (perhaps with a density or divisibility condition), phrased via the ternary relation 's is between a and b'. Thus the page records a reduction of the axiomatics of 'intervals as networks' to the classical axiomatics of betweenness. Recovering the order up to reversal from betweenness is indeed classical.
errors: No mathematical claim is completed, so there is nothing to refute.

Attribution is only roughly right. Betweenness axiomatics go back to Pasch (1882) and Hilbert's Grundlagen (1899, axioms of order). The characterization of linear orders up to reversal by a ternary betweenness relation is usually credited to Huntington and Kline (1917), with Veblen (1904) also relevant. For pairs not covered by S, the data S plus the components of L^ε must be shown to recover betweenness; the sketch does not check this.

ideas.what: Characterize an (ordered) interval, up to order reversal, by unordered combinatorial data: admissible pairs S ⊂ P_2(L) plus, for each pair, a 'connected component' decomposition of the common-neighbour set L^ε.
ideas.modern_name: Axiomatization of linear order via betweenness / separation (betweenness spaces, interval structures)

ideas.what: The Boolean algebra generated by mutually tame parts of a 1-dimensional tame space depends only on the finite subdivision ('découpage') by their boundary points (from p.39, used here as context).
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme (1984) sketches 'topologie modérée' only in general terms

missed.claim: Grothendieck abandons the exercise of characterizing an ordered interval as a 'réseau' via pair data and component decompositions. He defers to the classical betweenness axiomatics. This fragment belongs to his 1986 combinatorial approach to tame topology through 'découpages', which is itself largely unpublished.
missed.quote: J'ai commencé à faire l'exercice, mais j'ai l'impression que ce n'est pas la peine de l'expliciter jusqu'au bout. Ça doit avoir été fait depuis longtemps (Hilbert?)
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Mostly of historical interest. It shows he wanted a purely combinatorial (order-free) axiomatics of 1-dimensional tame strata, in the spirit of later o-minimal and combinatorial stratification theories. The mathematical content itself is classical.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a short, self-aborted exercise whose content (recovering order from betweenness) Grothendieck himself recognizes as classical. Its only interest is as context for his 1986 unpublished tame-topology program.
transcription_corrections: The symbol under S ⊂ P_2(L) reads like 'Drap_2(L)' or 'Drop_2(L)'; the reading is uncertain.
The subscript on L^ε is hard to read: it may be 'L_{und}' or 'L_{ε,d}' rather than 'L_ord'. The '[-L en-]' deletion is correctly struck.
The interlinear insertion above '(en termes d'une' looks like '(et divisible)' or 'cel divisibilité', possibly meaning dense ('divisible') order. It is not certainly 'divisibilité'.
The end reads: 'notion de la relation : s est entre a et b ...)'. This is consistent with the given transcription.
